exercises.label: Exercise 2.B1 — Medium: Certify a rectangular startup specification
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: The solution squares and sums both startup-coordinate bounds, shows the0.98 maximum and disk containment, derives coordinate magnitude from the Euclidean norm, identifies the symmetric A eigenvalues and contraction q, and propagates the worst radius. It also computes sharper row-wise0.49/0.56 bounds and translates them to the stated temperature units while explaining the locally valid-model induction. These are actual intermediate steps for all requested bounds.
exercises.replacement_html:
Cover every permitted startup. Here $P=I$, so the disk certificate is $V(x)=x_1^2+x_2^2\le1$. For any startup satisfying $|x_1|,|x_2|\le0.7$, square the coordinate bounds and add:

$$V(x_0)\le(0.7)^2+(0.7)^2=0.49+0.49=0.98\le1.$$

The maximum $0.98$ is attained at each startup-box corner. Thus the whole startup box, including its boundary, lies in the certified invariant disk. The nominal model is assumed exact inside the operating box; disk containment and invariance keep every subsequent state in that domain.

Obtain a uniform bound from the storage. Each coordinate magnitude is at most the vector's Euclidean norm, since $x_i^2\le x_1^2+x_2^2$. Therefore the energy calculation gives

$$|x_{i,0}|\le\|x_0\|_2\le\sqrt{0.98}\approx0.989949.$$

The original startup specification supplies the sharper initial coordinate bound $0.7$. The radius bound is useful because it does not depend on the direction of the state.

Propagate the radius one step. The symmetric matrix $A$ has characteristic equation $\lambda^2-1.3\lambda+0.41=0$, with eigenvalues $(13\pm\sqrt5)/20$. Both are positive, so its Euclidean induced norm is the larger one, $q=(13+\sqrt5)/20\approx0.761803$. Consequently,

$$|x_{i,1}|\le\|Ax_0\|_2\le q\|x_0\|_2 \le q\sqrt{0.98}\approx0.754147.$$

This is a valid common coordinate bound after one update. If we also use the rectangular startup information directly, the triangle inequality gives $|x_{1,1}|\le0.6(0.7)+0.1(0.7)=0.49$ and $|x_{2,1}|\le0.1(0.7)+0.7(0.7)=0.56$. Thus $0.56$ is a sharper common one-step bound for this particular startup box; the storage bound remains convenient for subsequent arbitrary directions.

Read the temperature units. Since $T_i=40+5x_i$, a dimensionless coordinate bound $b$ means $40-5b\le T_i\le40+5b$ degrees Celsius. The startup bound $0.7$ gives $36.5$–$43.5$ degrees, and the direct common one-step bound $0.56$ gives $37.2$–$42.8$ degrees. All are inside the permitted $35$–$45$ range.

exercises.label: Exercise 2.B2 — Hard: Replace convergence by a disturbance tube
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: The disturbance answer derives the norm recurrence by two explicit inequalities, maximizes it on a radius-R disk, rearranges and rationalizes R*=0.05/(1−q), and retains the operating-box restriction R≤1. It tests the unit disk, unrolls the recurrence and finite geometric sum, gives the ultimate rather than finite-entry conclusion, and constructs a nonzero equilibrium along the q eigenvector that both disproves universal convergence and proves smaller disks fail. No missing requested case remains.
exercises.replacement_html:
Include the disturbance at every step. Let $r_t=\|x_t\|_2$. The induced-norm bound for the stated $A$, followed by the triangle inequality, gives

$$r_{t+1}=\|Ax_t+w_t\|_2 \le\|Ax_t\|_2+\|w_t\|_2 \le q r_t+0.05,\qquad q=\frac{13+\sqrt5}{20}\lt1.$$

To make a disk of radius $R\ge0$ invariant, we need the right-hand side to be at most $R$ whenever $r_t\le R$. Since $q\ge0$, its largest value on that disk is $qR+0.05$. Solve

$$qR+0.05\le R \iff 0.05\le(1-q)R \iff R\ge R_*:=\frac{0.05}{1-q} =\frac{1}{7-\sqrt5} =\frac{7+\sqrt5}{44}\approx0.209911.$$

Division preserves the inequality because $1-q\gt0$. Every radius $R\ge R_*$ passes this algebraic norm test. To apply it using the lab's locally valid model, the disk must also lie inside the operating box; $R\le1$ is sufficient. Thus $R_*\le R\le1$ gives invariant disks fully covered by the stated model assumption. A larger disk may contain states outside that domain, so the norm calculation alone would not certify their updates. In particular, for $R=1$, $qR+0.05\approx0.811803\le1$, so the unit disk remains invariant for every disturbance in the given ball. As that disk lies in the operating box, induction also keeps the local model assumption applicable.

Show the transient and ultimate bounds. Iterating the scalar inequality yields $r_1\le qr_0+0.05$, $r_2\le q^2r_0+0.05(q+1)$, and in general

$$r_t\le q^t r_0+0.05\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}q^j =q^t r_0+\frac{0.05(1-q^t)}{1-q} =R_*+q^t(r_0-R_*).$$

The sum follows by multiplying the finite geometric sum by $q$ and subtracting it from the original sum. Because $q^t\to0$, this proves $\limsup_{t\to\infty}r_t\le R_*$. If a state starts outside the smallest disk, the bound approaches its radius; it does not assert entry into that exact disk in a finite number of steps.

Why convergence to zero is no longer guaranteed. Take a unit eigenvector $v$ of $A$ with $Av=qv$, and the allowed constant disturbance $w_t=0.05v$. At $x_*=R_*v$ we have

$$Ax_*+w_t=(qR_*+0.05)v=R_*v=x_*.$$

This nonzero equilibrium lies inside the unit disk and satisfies the model assumptions. Starting there produces a trajectory that never converges to zero. It also shows that no smaller centered Euclidean disk is robustly invariant: at the point $Rv$ with $R\lt R_*$ the same disturbance makes the next radius $qR+0.05\gt R$. The justified conclusion is an invariant disturbance tube and an ultimate bound. Convergence to zero would need further conditions, for example disturbances tending to zero.

exercises.label: Exercise 2.P1 — Easy: KKT with one active constraint
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: The original answer picks the nearest feasible point and verifies KKT, but does not solve the complementary-slackness alternatives. Show all four conditions, rule out an inactive bound by its infeasible stationary point, solve the active branch for λ, and give an elementary global/unique-optimum check alongside curvature.
exercises.replacement_html:
Set up the minimization with a consistent multiplier sign. The objective is $f(x)=(x-2)^2$, and the constraint is $g(x)=x-1\le0$. For this minimization use a nonnegative multiplier and

$$L(x,\lambda)=(x-2)^2+\lambda(x-1),\qquad\lambda\ge0.$$

The KKT conditions are

$$\begin{aligned} \text{stationarity: }&2(x-2)+\lambda=0,\\ \text{primal feasibility: }&x-1\le0,\\ \text{dual feasibility: }&\lambda\ge0,\\ \text{complementary slackness: }&\lambda(x-1)=0. \end{aligned}$$

Solve the possible slackness cases. If the bound were inactive, $x\lt1$ would make $x-1\ne0$, so complementary slackness would force $\lambda=0$. Stationarity would then give $2(x-2)=0$, hence $x=2$. That violates $x\le1$, so an inactive optimum is impossible.

The constraint must be active, giving $x=1$. Substitution into stationarity yields $2(1-2)+\lambda=0$, or $-2+\lambda=0$. Therefore

$$x^\star=1,\qquad\lambda^\star=2,\qquad f(x^\star)=(1-2)^2=1.$$

Verify and certify the result. Primal feasibility holds at equality; dual feasibility holds because $2\ge0$; stationarity is $-2+2=0$; and complementary slackness is $2(1-1)=0$. The objective has second derivative $f''(x)=2\gt0$ and the feasible half-line is convex, so these conditions give the unique global optimum. One can also see globality without invoking the theorem: for every feasible $x\le1$, $2-x\ge1$, so $(x-2)^2=(2-x)^2\ge1$, with equality only at $x=1$.

The positive multiplier reflects the binding constraint. The unconstrained minimum at $x=2$ would have value zero, but is excluded. If the bound is relaxed to $x\le1+\varepsilon$ with $0\lt\varepsilon\lt1$, the optimum value becomes $(1-\varepsilon)^2=1-2\varepsilon+\varepsilon^2$; its first-order improvement is $2\varepsilon$, consistent with multiplier $2$.
